audit_scope.description: Trust model analysis for batch 11 covering EIP-8123 (Gas Limit Cap Query), EIP-7823 (MODEXP Input Validation), EIP-627 (Whisper Protocol), Prague EOA Delegation (EIP-7702), and EIP-4788 (Beacon Root Storage)

components.name: Execution Layer (EL)
components.description: Ethereum execution layer processing transactions, smart contracts, and state transitions

components.name: Consensus Layer (CL)
components.description: Ethereum beacon chain consensus layer providing proof-of-stake consensus and block roots

misclassified_entities.reason: This represents contracts or EOAs making internal EVM calls, which are internal system components rather than truly external entities. These are part of the EL itself.
Smart contracts querying the beacon roots contract are internal to the EL, not external entities. They operate within the EVM execution environment.
While representing a threat actor, this is not an architectural entity but a threat model element. Attackers interact through legitimate external interfaces (users, RPC, etc.).
misclassified_entities.correct_classification: Threat actor, not an architectural entity

trusted_external_entities.name: Ethereum JSON-RPC Node Provider
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: JSON-RPC API (eth_txGasLimitCap and other RPC methods)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: RPC nodes provide information to clients but are not authenticated. Malicious or compromised nodes could return incorrect gas limit caps, causing transaction failures or preventing users from utilizing available gas. Clients must validate responses or use multiple providers.

trusted_external_entities.name: End User / Transaction Originator
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Transaction submission via wallet software or direct RPC calls
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Users submit transactions to the EL but are untrusted by design. The EL must validate all user inputs including signatures, nonces, gas limits, and transaction formats. Users can be malicious or make errors that could exploit vulnerabilities if not properly validated.

trusted_external_entities.name: Whisper Protocol Network Peer
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: DEVp2p network protocol with Whisper subprotocol (packet codes 0x00-0x03, 0x7E-0x7F)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Whisper peers are untrusted network participants that could send malformed packets, invalid proofs-of-work, expired messages, or attempt to perform traffic analysis. All envelope validation (structure, PoW, bloom filter matching) must be performed on received messages. Protocol violations should result in peer disconnection.

trusted_external_entities.name: Whisper-Enabled Application
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Whisper API for message submission and retrieval
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Applications using Whisper for private messaging are untrusted. They could submit messages with invalid parameters, attempt to decrypt messages not intended for them, or try to correlate traffic patterns. The Whisper layer must enforce cryptographic boundaries (ECIES, AES-GCM), apply padding to prevent size analysis, and validate all inputs.

trusted_external_entities.name: Beacon Chain Consensus Layer
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Engine API with JWT authentication providing parent_beacon_block_root in execution block headers
trusted_external_entities.rationale: The consensus layer is semi-trusted through the Engine API's JWT authentication mechanism. It provides beacon block roots that the EL uses without independent verification. This is a fundamental architectural trust boundary in post-merge Ethereum. If the CL is compromised or provides incorrect roots, the EL inherits that compromise. The authentication prevents unauthorized entities from injecting false beacon roots, but the EL trusts authenticated CL data.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: The EL does not trust RPC node responses. Clients querying RPC nodes must implement their own validation or use multiple providers to verify gas limit caps and other chain parameters. The EL's responsibility is to enforce correct protocol rules; it cannot prevent RPC nodes from lying to clients.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Transaction Mempool and Block Processing Pipeline
boundary_edges.security_assumption: All user transactions are untrusted and must pass comprehensive validation: ECDSA signature verification (including y_parity, r, s range checks for EIP-7702 authorizations), nonce validation, gas limit checks against protocol caps (EIP-8123), precompile input bounds (EIP-7823), and account state verification. Invalid transactions are rejected; validation failures should not crash the node.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: DEVp2p Network Layer with Whisper Subprotocol Handler
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Whisper peers are adversarial. All received envelopes must be validated for: correct structure [Expiry(4), TTL(4), Topic(4), Data(var), Nonce(8)], minimum proof-of-work requirements (not NaN, INF, or negative), and bloom filter topic matching. Invalid envelopes are silently dropped. Severe protocol violations (e.g., repeatedly sending expired messages) result in peer disconnection. Cryptographic validation (ECIES decryption) provides message authenticity.

Applications are untrusted. The Whisper layer enforces cryptographic boundaries: messages must be encrypted (ECIES asymmetric or AES-GCM symmetric) before transmission, signatures (ECDSA) are validated on receipt, and 256-byte alignment padding is applied to prevent size-based metadata leakage. Applications cannot access plaintext of messages not encrypted for their keys.

The CL is semi-trusted via JWT authentication. The EL trusts that authenticated CL connections provide correct parent_beacon_block_root values without independent verification. This is a fundamental trust boundary: the EL cannot validate beacon chain state independently and relies on CL honesty and correctness. JWT authentication prevents unauthorized injection of beacon roots, but the EL fully trusts authenticated data. Ring buffer storage (8191 entries) indexed by timestamp % HISTORY_BUFFER_LENGTH makes beacon roots available to smart contracts.

notes: Three entities were misclassified as external: EXT-CALLER and EXT-CALLING-CONTRACT are internal EL components (contracts/EOAs), and EXT-ATTACKER is a threat model element rather than an architectural entity.
EXT-BEACON-CHAIN is semantically identical to EXT-CONSENSUS-LAYER (both refer to the beacon chain), so they were consolidated into a single entity EXT-CONSENSUS-LAYER.
The CL-to-EL boundary is critical: it represents the post-merge architectural trust boundary where beacon chain data enters the execution layer via authenticated Engine API.
All truly external entities (RPC nodes, users, Whisper peers, Whisper applications, and consensus layer) have been analyzed with appropriate trust levels and boundary edges defined.
The batch covers a diverse set of EIPs: RPC query protocol (8123), precompile security (7823), P2P messaging (627), EOA enhancement (7702), and CL-EL integration (4788).
